extracted.intended_audience: naturalists, geologists, and educated general readers interested in physical geography and volcanology
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and descriptive criteria for classifying volcanoes, interpreting their structure and products, and identifying signs and causes of volcanic activity based on field observation and comparative geology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification: central versus linear volcanoes
rubrics_metrics.description: Volcanoes are characteristically classified as central (a central point with many active mouths distributed almost regularly in all directions) or linear (separate vents or chimneys lying along an extended fissure). Linear volcanoes admit further subdivision into conical islands rising from the sea floor, and volcanic chains elevated on mountain ridges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Peak of Teneriffe is a central volcano; the Andes are a long rampart-like continental volcanic chain. Note debates/nuances (Darwin, Von Buch) and intermediate forms where fissures intersect (Lipari group).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation of elevation to eruption frequency
rubrics_metrics.description: Eruptions are generally more frequent in low volcanoes than in loftier ones; if volcanic foci are at equal depth, greater elevation of the mountain requires greater force to erupt, reducing frequency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: Stromboli (2318 ft) incessantly active; Vesuvius and Aetna less frequently; Cotopaxi (19,069 ft) with long intervals between eruptions. Exceptions occur when channels of communication vary in permanence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cone of cinders and crater dimensions independent of mountain size
rubrics_metrics.description: Height of the cone of cinders and the size/shape of the crater impart individual character to volcanoes and are independent of the dimensions of the whole mountain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example ratios: Vesuvius' cone of cinders is one-third of the mountain's height, while the Peak of Teneriffe's cone is 1/22nd. Avoid conflating cone of eruption openings with the enclosing crater.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crater depth and bottom activity as eruption indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: The greater or lesser depth of the crater, and the condition of its bottom (opening/closing fissures, hollows filled with molten masses, cones rising and falling), are often signs of near or distant occurrence of an eruption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe long narrow fissures, ascending vapors, formation of scoriae cones within the crater, and small local earthquakes that precede visible activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eruptions commonly occur from lateral fissures
rubrics_metrics.description: Eruptions from the summit crater are unusual in many mountains; lava and material frequently erupt from lateral fissures whenever the sides of the upheaved mountain are least able to resist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical example: Aetna in the 16th century (Bembo). Lateral fissure eruptions may form cones of eruption on the sides.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cones of eruption (including 'hornitos' and 'new volcanoes')
rubrics_metrics.description: Cones uplifted on fissures may appear as larger cones aligned along fissures (sometimes called 'new volcanoes') or as clusters of smaller dome-like or hive-shaped cones ('hornitos') covering a district.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'hornitos de Jorullo', cone of Vesuvius (1822), Awatscha, lava-field cones near Baidar Mountains. Note that some of these small cones can disappear or change form over decades.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local topography and elevation influence lava-stream formation
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether lava streams form and extend beyond the crater depends on local conditions such as the surrounding plateau elevation and the mountain's form, position, and height; some high plateau volcanoes produce little or no lava streams despite violent eruptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: volcanoes of the Andes of Quito surrounded by tableland (9,000–13,000 ft) often show eruptions of ignited scoriae without major lava streams; Java provides counterexamples, so other factors also matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lava and volcanic product composition depends on rock type, eruption height, and internal temperature
rubrics_metrics.description: The mineral composition of lava varies with the crystalline rock forming the volcano, the altitude of the eruption (foot vs crater), and the internal temperature; vitreous formations (obsidian, pumice) may be absent or restricted to high eruption points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These relations require accurate crystallographic and chemical investigations (e.g., Gustav Rose, Hermann Abich).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fumaroles and vapors: steam predominance and sublimation products
rubrics_metrics.description: The greater part of ascending vapor from volcanoes is steam; fumaroles cause sublimation of chlorides of iron, copper, lead, and ammonium, and cavities and fissures may be lined with chlorides and salts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: sodium chloride found in cavities of recent lava streams; Pantellaria hot springs used by goatherds; reference to chemical studies (Mitscherlich, Gay-Lussac).

rubrics_metrics.name: Volcanic products can include metals and salts
rubrics_metrics.description: Some volcanoes yield metallic and salt products among their emissions—iron, copper, lead, arsenic, selenium have been found in volcanic craters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Stromeyer discovered these metals in the crater of Volcano (island near Lipari); boracic acid and silky crystals reported on some islands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Volcanic storm: cloud formation, increased electric tension, and lightning
rubrics_metrics.description: Eruptions produce columns of steam and cinders that condense into large clouds, increasing atmospheric electric tension; forked lightning may flash from the volcanic cloud and rolling thunder of the volcanic storm is distinguishable from internal detonations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notable observations: Vesuvius (Oct 1822), Katlagia eruption (Iceland, 1755) where lightning from volcanic cloud killed animals and people. Distinguish these atmospheric electrical effects from interior explosions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between volcanic and plutonic rock formation based on pressure during solidification
rubrics_metrics.description: The main difference between plutonic and volcanic rocks is the greater or lesser pressure under which softened or wholly liquid matter is solidified; subterranean forces also sever old combinations of matter to produce new ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This conceptual distinction explains differing textures and structures of igneous products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and behavior of lava currents and solidification
rubrics_metrics.description: The mineral mass flowing from a volcanic opening is called lava; when many currents meet and are arrested they expand and solidify in superimposed strata, filling basins; quiet, well-defined terrestrial streams can keep the crater accessible even during eruptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observation of lava flow morphology and resulting stratification provides insight into eruption dynamics and ensuing landscape.

rubrics_metrics.name: Water and mud ejections from mountain hollows are indirectly related to volcanic activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Hot water and mud flowing from hollows in trachytic mass (not from crater) are only indirectly connected to volcanic activity; infiltration of melted snow can produce subterranean reservoirs that may be suddenly opened during earthquakes, ejecting water, fish, and mud.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ejections of fish in highlands of Quito (prenadilla), 1698 collapse of Carguairazo yielding lodazales; such phenomena resemble 'volcanic storms' but are distinct from direct eruptive products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observable pre-eruption signs: fusion of snow, glowing cone walls, ascending vapors, small earthquakes
rubrics_metrics.description: Imminent eruptions may be preceded by sudden fusion of snow at the cone, glowing heat in the walls of the cone of cinders, smoke in rarefied strata, ascending vapors and opening/closing of hollows, often announced by small local earthquakes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These field signs are useful early indicators; observers should note thermal changes, vapor emission patterns, and seismic precursors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crater margin stability over long periods (marginal ledges vary less than supposed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Marginal ledges of craters often remain stable over long periods; comparative measurements (Saussure and Humboldt) showed little change in Vesuvius' margin elevation over 49 years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use careful repeated measurement to assess actual geomorphic change rather than relying on fanciful descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Volcanic edifices can form by sudden elevation (craters of elevation) rather than by accumulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Many volcanic mountains are not formed by gradual accumulation of ejected lava but by sudden elevation of soft masses (craters of elevation); some 'new mountains' (e.g., Jorullo) result from uplift rather than extensive lava outpouring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical and classical descriptions (Ovid, Plato, Aristotle) contain analogies to these phenomena; distinguish craters of elevation from true eruptive accumulative cones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proximity and alignment of volcanoes indicate subterranean communications
rubrics_metrics.description: Groups and chains of volcanoes often show mutual dependence and alignment that reflect deep-seated subterranean communications and fissures; activity may propagate along such directions for centuries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Mexican highlands alignment (Orizaba, Popocatepetl, Jorullo, Colima) lie in a transverse fissure; Seneca and classical writers anticipated the idea of subterranean communication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cautious use of historical/mythical accounts for geognostic interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Ancient myths and classical descriptions (Plato's Pyriphlegethon, Ovid, Aristotle) can offer suggestive imagery but must be critically interpreted, as they may conflate different phenomena (e.g., pumice-mixed snow-mud mistaken for mud eruptions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare classical accounts to observed local phenomena (e.g., salses, mud volcanoes) and avoid literal acceptance; use them as historical clues rather than scientific proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid conflating cones of eruption with enclosing crater
rubrics_metrics.description: Openings that rise from the bottom of the crater (cones of eruption) are distinct from the crater that incloses them; these features should not be confused when describing crater morphology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Careful field description and mapping should distinguish crater rim, crater floor hollows, and intra-crater cones to avoid misinterpretation of eruptive structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mineralogical and chemical study required to explain volatile relations and product distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Explaining the presence/absence of certain volcanic materials (e.g., obsidian, pumice, salts, metals) and the chemical origin of sublimates requires detailed crystallographic and chemical investigations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reference and rely on rigorous analyses (e.g., Berzelius, Wohler, Gay-Lussac, Bischof) rather than solely on macroscopic field observation.
